evidence.note: Works through the contract subsystem-by-subsystem, creating a dedicated route file per area (auth, users, workspaces, channels, messages, extra, irc) — an implicit ordered coverage map of the API surface, keeping distinct areas from being lost.

'the backend appears functionally complete according to the provided specifications' — declares a whole subsystem done based on having written the code, conflating 'wrote the route' with verified-against-contract (the anchor-3 failure mode); no functional API/WS/IRC testing backs this claim.

Genuine coverage reconciliation: 'revisited the requirements document', 'auditing the necessary data-testid attributes', 'confirmed the presence of auth-form/auth-toggle...', then 'Identifying Missing Components... all of which are missing' — an active testid checklist that detects gaps and triggers writing Settings.jsx to fill them.

Final spot-checks against specific spec items (hashtag prefixes, avatars, resilience/cross-node write success) — but these are ad-hoc prose confirmations, not a maintained ledger; status codes (409/413/423), all WS frame kinds, IRC numerics, and seq-density are never revisited for verification coverage.

reasoning: The agent keeps a usable, mostly-implicit running picture of the contract — organizing work by subsystem, revisiting the requirements doc, and running a real testid audit that catches missing UI components (steps 58-64) — matching the level-5 description of a usable running list where current state is generally known. But tracking is prose-based rather than an explicit ledger, and verification status is loosely handled: it repeatedly treats 'wrote the file' as 'complete' (step 28) and never systematically reconciles the fine-grained contract items (status codes, WS kinds, IRC numerics, seq density) against actual verification, falling well short of the explicit implemented-vs-verified ledger at level 8. The UI-testid coverage work lifts it above a pure 3.
